opus-5.5.text:
I think it's probably not going to be that useful for verifying code in the traditional sense, at least not directly. The thing I'm most interested in is a pretty different use case.

When people think about formal verification of code, the goal is usually a proof that a program satisfies some specification, like this function always returns a sorted list, or this system never enters an unsafe state. And there's already a lot of good work there. A heuristic estimator isn't a proof. It gives you something more like a reasonable best guess given the arguments you've considered. So if what you want is the kind of airtight guarantee you get from formal methods, this isn't that, and I wouldn't pitch it as a replacement.

What I'm actually hoping for is something more like this. You have a neural network, and you observe that it behaves well on the training distribution. You'd like to understand *why* it behaves well, in the sense of having an explanation, maybe a heuristic argument, that accounts for that good behavior. Then when you deploy it and see a new input, you can ask: is the model still behaving well for the same reason? Or is something different happening on this input, some mechanism that wasn't present in the explanation you had for training? That's the setting where I think heuristic estimation could matter a lot, for things like mechanistic anomaly detection, or catching cases where a model's behavior is driven by something we didn't anticipate, like a treacherous turn.

Now, there's some overlap with code. A neural network is a program, after all. And you could imagine applying similar ideas to ordinary software: you have a bunch of tests that pass, you have some argument for why the code works, and you want to flag inputs where the code is doing something outside the scope of that argument. I think that's plausible and could be somewhat useful. But for a lot of ordinary software, the humans who wrote it already have a pretty good understanding of why it works, and the tools we have, testing, type systems, formal verification for the high-stakes cases, are reasonably well suited to that. The distinctive thing about neural nets is that nobody understands why they work, and there isn't a human-written explanation sitting around. That's the gap I'm trying to fill.

I'd also say, honestly, we're still pretty far from having a heuristic estimator that works well in general. A lot of what we're doing is trying to figure out what the right formalization even is, and whether it's possible to define something that behaves sensibly across a broad range of cases. So I'd put the code verification question as a possible side benefit, maybe, if things go well, not the main thing I'd bet on.

r001.rationale: The response describes formal verification as proving specifications, but does not identify formalizing proofs as a major bottleneck for verifying much code.

r002.rationale: It says the estimator is not a proof or a replacement for formal methods, but does not specifically predict that it will not help with the difficulty of formalizing proofs.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention simulation-based code or controlling numerical error.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I want to be honest about where this sits in my own thinking. The reason I'm working on heuristic estimators, or heuristic arguments more broadly, is not primarily because I think they'll be a great tool for verifying code in the near term. The motivation is about mechanistic anomaly detection and eliciting latent knowledge, about being able to say something about why a neural network does what it does without the kind of airtight proof that formal verification demands. Code verification is kind of a side benefit, or maybe a sanity check on whether the whole project makes sense.

That said, I think there's a real story here. The core problem with formal verification is that for most interesting programs, you can't prove the thing you care about. Either the property isn't precisely specified, or it's true only in some probabilistic sense, or the proof would be astronomically long. What a heuristic estimator is supposed to do is let you say "here is an argument that this program behaves correctly on typical inputs, and here's roughly how confident that argument should make you," and then have that argument be checkable and composable in the way proofs are. You'd be able to take a hash function and argue it looks like a random function, take a sorting routine and argue it does the right thing on the distribution you care about, and chain those together without ever producing a proof.

So if you ask me whether this is going to replace testing or static analysis in the next five years, I'd say almost certainly not. The formal machinery isn't there. We don't even have a satisfying definition of what a heuristic estimator is, let alone an implementation that works on real code. I'd put a lot of probability on the whole research program failing on its own terms, in the sense that we never find an estimator with the properties we want.

But conditional on it working, I think it would be fairly useful for code. The reason is that the gap between "we tested it and it seemed fine" and "we proved it correct" is enormous, and most real software lives in that gap. A tool that let you give structured, inspectable reasons for believing a program is correct, where those reasons could be checked by a machine and where the machine would tell you when your argument has a hole in it, that's something people would use. Especially in a world where AI systems are writing most of the code and you'd like some handle on whether to trust it beyond "the model said it's fine."

I'd also flag that the most important application for me isn't really verifying code that humans write. It's verifying the models themselves, treating the neural network as the program and asking whether its behavior on the deployment distribution is explained by the same mechanism as its behavior on the training distribution. If you can do that, you've got a way of noticing when a model is doing something qualitatively new, which is most of what I care about from a safety perspective. Ordinary code verification is the easier, more legible version of that problem, and if we can't make progress there, I'd take it as fairly bad news for the harder version.

r001.rationale: The response says formal verification fails for many interesting programs because properties may be imprecise or probabilistic, or the proof may be astronomically long.

r002.rationale: It doubts the estimator’s near-term readiness and says the research program may fail, but does not predict that it will fail to help with formalizing proofs for code verification.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss simulation-based code or numerical error control.

astra-6.text:
I think code is a particularly promising case, because you have a relatively precise thing you’re trying to establish. You can ask, “What’s the probability that this program does something other than what this specification says?” And you’d like your estimator to recognize arguments that make that probability very small, even when it can’t produce a formal proof.

The tricky part is that passing a bunch of tests is usually not enough. There could be some very rare input on which the program fails, or an input that someone deliberately constructs to make it fail. So you need the estimator to do more than extrapolate from the cases you’ve seen. It needs to understand something about why the program works.

If we had a good heuristic estimator, I’d hope it could bridge that gap between testing and formal verification. But that’s a hope about what the framework could deliver, rather than something we’ve demonstrated. A lot depends on whether you can actually build an estimator that recognizes the relevant reasoning without also being confidently wrong in ways an adversary can exploit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could be useful, but it depends on what you mean by verifying code. If you mean producing a proof that a program satisfies some formal specification, then you still need to write down that specification, and you need a proof that a checker can actually check. A heuristic estimator doesn’t automatically solve either of those problems.

The thing I’d be excited about is using it to estimate whether a program has a bug, even when you can’t afford to explore all the possible executions. You’d like to be able to take an argument like, “This change shouldn’t affect that part of the program,” and ask how much confidence that argument really gives you. And then combine lots of those arguments without accidentally counting the same evidence many times.

But that’s an aspiration. The hard question is whether we can make those estimates reliable on complicated cases where we don’t already know the answer. So I’d distinguish the potential application, which seems quite valuable, from how much we’ve demonstrated, which is much more limited.

r001.rationale: It mentions writing a specification and a checkable proof, but does not identify formalizing proofs as a major bottleneck for verifying a substantial portion of code.

r002.rationale: It says the estimator does not automatically solve the problem of writing down a specification or producing a checkable proof, communicating that it will not address the formalization difficulty.

r003.rationale: It discusses estimating bug risk and combining arguments, but does not predict usefulness for simulation-based code or controlling numerical error.
